system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Topologically associating domains
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers TADs as intervals of high internal contact frequency defined by chromosome conformation capture, their relation to compartments, CTCF-oriented loop bases and cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, and the caveat that population-averaged data do not show contacts in every cell. Excludes experimental protocol details of 3C variants.

ATOMS:
- MED-EPI-C10-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Intervals of chromatin with high internal contact frequencies are termed topologically associating domains (TADs).
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s11] Intervals with high internal contact frequencies are termed topologically associating domains (TADs, 7 Method Box 1.3).
- MED-EPI-C10-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are confined by borders that limit interactions, so that high frequencies of interaction are observed within a TAD and little interaction is observed outside it.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0038-s23] Topological associated domains (TADs) (right) are confined by borders that limit interactions.
    [MED-EPI-p0038-s24] High frequencies of interactions are observed within TADs and little interactions are observed outside.
- MED-EPI-C10-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Studies of in vivo 3D chromosome topology using chromatin conformation capture have shown that chromosomes are made up of domains of interacting chromatin that are partitioned by boundaries between them.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s09] Using this approach, the in vivo 3D topology of chromosomes has been investigated.
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s10] From these studies it has become apparent that chromosomes are made up of domains of interacting chromatin that are partitioned by boundaries between them.
- MED-EPI-C10-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: A number of topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries can be correlated with CTCF binding sites.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0039-s14] A number of TAD boundaries can be correlated with CTCF binding sites.
- MED-EPI-C10-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Cohesins are loaded on chromatin in interphase and likely can slide along the chromatin fiber, mediating loop formation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0039-s10] Cohesins are loaded on chromatin in interphase and likely can slide along the chromatin fiber, mediating loop formation.
- MED-EPI-C10-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: CTCF sites at the base of chromatin loops are oriented towards each other.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0039-s13] CTCF sites at the base of chromatin loops are oriented towards each other, suggesting that CTCF might act in a directional manner to block cohesin sliding.
- MED-EPI-C10-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Chromatin conformation capture (3C) and related techniques usually investigate several thousands to millions of cells, so only population averages of contacts are observed, even though TADs might share regulatory elements and be co-regulated.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s12] Although TADs might share regulatory elements and be co-regulated, it is important to realize that 3C and related techniques usually investigate a large number – several thousands to millions – of cells and, therefore, only averages are observed.
- MED-EPI-C10-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: A-compartments predominantly consist of sequences correlated with active chromatin marks and can be distinguished from B-compartments, which contain largely inactive chromatin and frequently locate to the nuclear periphery.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s18] A-compartments predominantly consist of sequences that are correlated with active chromatin marks.
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s19] These can be distinguished from B-compartments that contain largely inactive chromatin and frequently locate to the nuclear periphery.
- MED-EPI-C10-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: It is not always clear whether, in a given cell at a given time, all of the contacts detected by 3C techniques take place.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s12] Although TADs might share regulatory elements and be co-regulated, it is important to realize that 3C and related techniques usually investigate a large number – several thousands to millions – of cells and, therefore, only averages are observed.
    [MED-EPI-p0037-s13] It is not always clear whether, in a given cell at a given time, all contacts take place. 3C techniques have been very successful in identifying gene regulatory elements such as enhancers that are located at a distance from their promoters but show a high contact frequency.
